title: Profiling the Attack Surface of AI Agent Skills
content:
Computer Science > Cryptography and Security
  [Submitted on 13 Oct 2026]
Title:Beyond Maliciousness: Static and Runtime Attack-Surface Profiling of Agent Skills
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Agent skills are Markdown documents that a tool-using agent reads as instructions and then acts on with the privileges of the session that loaded them. Installing one grants authority (the standing to direct the agent, not new privilege), and the size of that grant is what we measure. We present a two-phase attack-surface profiling methodology that combines whole-bundle static analysis and dependency provenance checking with instrumented sandbox execution and separate model-based assessment of the resulting traces. We apply the methodology to 6,309 listings from two marketplaces, selecting listings for execution without conditioning that decision on a prior threat or risk signal. Half the corpus carries evidence of shell-execution capability; the corresponding shares are 35% for filesystem read, 31% each for filesystem write and network egress, and 13% for credential access; seven listings in ten carry at least one elevated capability. That is the surface a user accepts at install time, and almost none of it is visible then. A permission model exists but is close to inert. Authors may list the tools a skill pre-approves in its own frontmatter, which removes confirmation prompts rather than restricting what the skill can reach; of the 6,061 listings whose frontmatter parses, 770 declare anything at all, the vocabulary cannot express credential or environment access, and nothing checks what it does express against the bundle. Declaring is also not declaring accurately: 59% of declaring listings understate what their bundle can do. ClawHub declares roughly twice as often as skillsmp, yet under-declares on 88% of its declarations against 31%. Triage at the marketplace boundary therefore cannot rest on what a listing declares. It must rest on what the bundle can do. These results position capability-oriented attack-surface profiling as a necessary complement to maliciousness detection.

report.summary: A large-scale study of 6,309 agent-skill marketplace listings finds most bundles can execute shell commands, read files, or reach the network, yet self-declared permissions are near-useless and routinely understated.
report.background: Agent skills are lightweight Markdown instruction bundles that tool-using LLM agents load and then act on with the full privileges of the hosting session. Marketplaces such as ClawHub and skillsmp have grown quickly because skills are trivially easy to author and install, creating an ecosystem that mirrors early browser extensions or npm packages — huge, fast-moving, and largely unaudited. Existing security work has focused on detecting deliberately malicious skills (prompt injection, credential theft), but the authors argue this framing misses a broader problem: even a well-intentioned skill may grant itself shell execution, filesystem access, or network egress simply because nothing constrains it. A nominal permission model exists in the form of frontmatter declarations, but the paper shows it is poorly specified, unverified, and often inaccurate. The research lands as enterprises begin deploying agents with real credentials and infrastructure access, making install-time trust decisions a genuine supply-chain question rather than a curiosity.
key_points: The attack surface is the default, not the exception: half of the 6,309 listings showed evidence of shell-execution capability, roughly a third could read or write files or send data over the network, 13% could reach credentials, and seven in ten carried at least one elevated capability — almost none of it visible at install time.

The permission model is close to inert. A skill can pre-approve tools in its own frontmatter, but this removes user confirmation prompts instead of limiting what the skill can actually reach, and the vocabulary cannot even express credential or environment access.

Declarations are rare and unreliable. Of 6,061 listings with parsable frontmatter, only 770 declare anything at all, and 59% of those understate what their bundle can do. ClawHub declares about twice as often as skillsmp but under-declares on 88% of its declarations versus 31%.

The authors built a two-phase methodology: whole-bundle static analysis plus dependency provenance checking, then instrumented sandbox execution with separate model-based assessment of the resulting traces. Listings were selected for execution without conditioning on any prior threat or risk signal.

The conclusion is that marketplace triage cannot rely on what a listing claims, only on what its bundle can actually do — making capability-oriented attack-surface profiling a necessary complement to maliciousness detection.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes agent-skill security from a malware-hunting problem to a permissions and supply-chain problem, and it suggests marketplaces will need automated capability extraction at upload time rather than self-attestation. For developers, it means a skill is a privilege grant, not a config file: sandbox execution, least-privilege sessions, and provenance checks on dependencies should become standard before any third-party bundle touches production credentials. For regular users, the practical takeaway is uncomfortable — installing a skill is closer to running an unsigned installer than adding a plugin, and the confirmation prompts they see reflect declarations that are frequently wrong. Expect pressure toward signed bundles, manifest standards that can express credential scope, and runtime capability monitors.
report.tools: Worth following: ClawHub and skillsmp (the studied marketplaces), the Model Context Protocol for tool-permission patterns, sandbox runtimes such as gVisor, Firecracker, and E2B for instrumented execution, static analyzers like Semgrep and CodeQL for bundle scanning, SLSA and Sigstore for dependency provenance and signing, and OpenSSF Scorecard for supply-chain hygiene. LLM Guard and garak help with prompt-injection and model-level testing, while the paper's two-phase profiling method is the blueprint to reimplement.
